- Shared method: both papers probe ChatGPT's internal organization by eliciting *repeated, patterned generations* rather than single one-off outputs
  - Reference paper: asks ChatGPT for 20 versions of the same prototypical story
  - Subject paper's own experiment (per sidenote): asks ChatGPT for "20 things," then "50 more," tracking how the list drifts
- Both treat repetition/variation across trials as a probe into latent conceptual/ontological structure, not just narrative style
  - Reference paper: variation across the 20 story versions reveals stable vs. flexible narrative elements
  - Subject paper: variation across list items reveals category drift (xxx-fly pattern -> flying bugs -> general bugs -> flying mammals -> general mammals), i.e. ChatGPT's ontology has abstraction levels
- Both surface a bias/attractor effect under sustained querying
  - Reference paper's "short note on method" documents how repeated prompting settles into recurring patterns (a prototypical story)
  - Subject paper's "20 Questions" test finds an analogous asymmetry: yes/no questions favor the less frequent (abstract) option, and list generation collapses toward broader/more general categories over more iterations
- Reference paper functions as methodological precedent/companion evidence
  - It legitimizes the subject paper's core technique (mass-sampling ChatGPT outputs to infer hidden structure)
  - Its focus on "prototypical story" complements the subject paper's focus on "ontological landscape": one maps narrative prototypes, the other maps conceptual/category prototypes
